title: T1608.002 — Stage Capabilities - Upload Tool
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Stage Capabilities - Upload Tool with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Animated diagram: an attacker uploads tools to a private code-host repository, a phishing link compromises a workstation, the implant beacons out, pulls the staged tool, and moves to a second server, while the SOC catches the pull and responds.

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: The threat actor. Packs the toolkit and waits for a foothold inside the target.

nodes.label: Staged store
nodes.tip: A code-hosting or cloud-drive account that keeps the tools until an implant asks for them.

nodes.label: Workstation
nodes.tip: A compromised office computer. Its implant decides when to pull the staged tools.

nodes.label: File server
nodes.tip: A second internal server. Attackers pull tools onto it during lateral movement.

nodes.label: SOC analyst
nodes.tip: The defender. Joins proxy, EDR, and DNS telemetry to catch the tool pull.

steps.title: Pack the toolkit
steps.caption: In their own lab, the operator packs three generic tools: a remote-admin client, a tunneling binary, and a credential dumper. Nothing has touched the target yet.
steps.defender: No victim-side evidence exists. Build and pack machines belong to the attacker, so your logs stay quiet.

steps.title: Create the private repo
steps.caption: The operator creates a fresh account on a public code-hosting platform and a private repository with a release page. This is where the toolkit will wait.
steps.defender: A brand-new account appears on a public code host. OSINT watchlists can flag fresh accounts that later host releases, but private files stay invisible.

steps.title: Upload the toolkit
steps.caption: The operator uploads the three tools as release assets. One staged copy can now serve many victims, and nothing heavy has to ship inside the phishing payload.
steps.defender: Nothing visible yet: the files are private and no victim has touched them. Hash feeds usually learn a staged tool only after the first download by some victim.

steps.title: First foothold by phishing
steps.caption: A phishing link tricks an employee into running a tiny dropper on workstation FIN-WKS-0142. The dropper is small on purpose - the heavy tools will arrive later, on demand.
steps.defender: The mail gateway logs the click, and EDR sees only a small 92 KB dropper. No big tool exists on disk yet, so the incident still looks minor.

steps.title: Implant beacons out
steps.caption: The dropper becomes a quiet implant. It sends small call-home messages - beacons - to learn its tasks, including the address where the toolkit waits.
steps.defender: A rare domain with very low volume appears: a few kilobytes per hour. This is easy to miss without traffic baselines and rare-domain rules.

steps.title: Implant pulls the tool
steps.caption: The implant fetches the tunneling binary from the staged release and saves it under C:\Users\Public. The staged tool has now crossed into your network.
steps.defender: The smoking gun: proxy shows an office workstation pulling a binary from a code-host raw path. EDR logs the file write. Two independent signals at last.

fields.detail: The implant fetches the tunneling binary from the staged release and saves it under C:\Users\Public.

detection.label: Partial signal
detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: Tool runs, lateral move
steps.caption: The tool executes, and the attacker reaches a second server, FS-02, in the data-center VLAN. There they install a service for persistence.
steps.defender: EDR raises a chain alert - downloader, new tool, then a new service on FS-02. Servers fetching executables is behavior that should never happen.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: SOC response
steps.caption: The SOC isolates both hosts, removes the tools and persistence, blocks the staging URL, and rotates the credentials that were exposed.
steps.defender: Hunting finds the same toolkit hash on one more host - caught before it ran. The staging account is reported for abuse, burning the attacker's setup.
